claims.text: The starting material is a duplex-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating.
Rapid cooling produces relatively incoherent and widely spaced FCC/BCC interphase boundaries in the starting coating.
Tailored heat treatment can increase FCC/BCC interphase-boundary coherency.
Tailored heat treatment can reduce the spacing of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
Greater FCC/BCC interphase-boundary coherency produces localized interfacial stress or strain fields.
Localized interfacial stress fields hinder dislocation nucleation and motion.
Improved boundary coherency induces misfit-dislocation networks at FCC/BCC interfaces.
The interfacial strain fields and misfit-dislocation networks impede both dislocation glide and climb.
The resulting interfacial barrier delays progressive plastic deformation and improves creep resistance under sustained loading.
Creep testing between 0.4 and 0.6 Tm represents service-relevant sustained-loading conditions for the proposed coating.
Diffusion-activated processes are limited between approximately 0.4 and 0.6 Tm.
Heat-treated samples with more coherent and closely spaced boundaries will have a significantly lower creep strain rate than the rapidly cooled baseline.
Heat-treated samples will enter tertiary creep later than the baseline samples.
The boundary-coherency mechanism is expected to operate primarily between 0.4 and 0.6 Tm.
Outside the proposed temperature range, diffusion-dominated creep or other strengthening mechanisms may confound the effect of interphase-boundary coherency.
Precipitate strengthening may make an uncertain contribution to creep resistance relative to the proposed interphase-boundary mechanism.
Greater interface coherency should correlate with altered or reduced dislocation activity near the phase boundaries.
A lack of statistically significant creep-rate reduction or tertiary-creep delay, or a lack of correlation between coherency and interfacial dislocation activity, would falsify the hypothesis.
